strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely problem: jailbreak benchmarks become stale relative to rapidly evolving attack literature, and the paper offers a concrete, well-engineered pipeline (planner–coder–auditor) to close this gap.

Extensive empirical validation across 30 diverse attacks and 10 victim models under a single harness/judge, which is a substantial engineering and evaluation effort; the resulting ASR heatmap (Fig. 4) enables genuinely new cross-attack/cross-model observations (e.g., mechanism-specific bypasses, carrier-format sensitivity, limited transferability).

Careful ablations beyond the headline fidelity number: with-repo vs. no-repo reproduction, iteration-count vs. ASR correlation analysis (showing no spurious correlation), and a targeted 'enhanced refinement pass' analysis that isolates implementation-driven failure modes from irreducible paper ambiguity.

Reasonable and interpretable engineering metrics (42% LOC compression, 82.5% code reuse) that support the claim of reduced integration burden, with concrete examples (RENELLM, DEEPINCEPTION, GTA) explaining variance in compression.

Very high transparency: full agent prompts, auditor acceptance criteria, and complexity/runtime breakdowns are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the pipeline itself (modulo access to the same proprietary agent backends).
weaknesses: The headline '+0.26pp mean ASR deviation' understates the actual spread: per-attack deviations range from -16.0 to +20.0 pp, and several attacks (SCP, ISA, TAP, TrojFill) show double-digit gaps; framing this as 'high fidelity' in the abstract is somewhat optimistic given the variance, and no statistical dispersion (e.g., std, MAE) is reported alongside the mean.

The auditor is explicitly static-only (never executes code; Appendix B.6) and acceptance is based on an LLM's line-referenced self-assessment against a plan it also helped shape; there is no independent human or execution-based verification of the reported 100%-fidelity acceptances, which weakens confidence in the auditing loop's actual reliability beyond the post-hoc ASR check.

Comparisons to 'general-purpose paper-to-code agents' failing on jailbreak reproduction (Section 2/3.2) are asserted but never empirically demonstrated with a baseline; a direct head-to-head against a generic paper-to-code agent (e.g., PaperCoder-style) would substantiate the claimed necessity of the specialized JBF-FORGE design.

Standardized JBF-EVAL results rely entirely on a single GPT-4o judge for all 30 attacks across 10 models; judge-victim overlap and judge reliability/agreement with human or original-paper judges are not analyzed, which could bias comparative claims about model robustness and attack transfer in Section 5.

The system depends on specific commercial/proprietary agent stacks (Cursor Agent with Gemini-3-pro/Claude-4.5-sonnet/GPT-5.1 Codex, plus Claude Code for refinement); this makes exact reproduction of the reported 28.2-minute synthesis times and fidelity numbers difficult for others without matching access, and no ablation isolates how much of the reported fidelity depends on these specific (state-of-the-art, likely expensive) model choices versus the pipeline design itself.

The dual-use/ethics discussion is brief and somewhat generic ('we advocate responsible deployment'); given that the paper explicitly demonstrates a system that can synthesize working, tuned jailbreak code from a paper in ~28 minutes with minimal human effort, a more substantive treatment of release/access controls (e.g., whether/how the tool or generated modules will be gated) would be warranted.

Attack/paper selection is restricted to those reporting on AdvBench or JBB with retrievable settings, and 'representative setting' selection (one victim/config per paper) is a simplification that may not generalize to the full space of settings papers report, potentially cherry-picking favorable conditions for fidelity matching.

strengths: Substantial engineering effort: a full multi-agent (planner-coder-auditor) pipeline, a shared contract library (JBF-LIB), and a standardized evaluation harness (JBF-EVAL) are built and applied to 30 attacks across 10 victim models, producing a large, useful artifact for the community.

The empirical coverage is broad: a 30-attack x 10-model ASR matrix under a unified harness is a valuable resource that surfaces genuine phenomena (e.g., GPT-OSS-120B's narrow blind spots, carrier-format sensitivity differences across models) that smaller/stale benchmarks would miss.

The paper is transparent about its pipeline internals, providing full agent prompts, acceptance criteria, and a complexity/timing analysis (Appendices B-H), which aids understanding of how the system works.

Honest reporting of failure cases (e.g., SCP, ISA under-reproduction; the non-improving ISA refinement case) and an iteration-count-vs-ASR correlation analysis showing no significant relationship, rather than cherry-picking only favorable results.
weaknesses: Circularity in the core fidelity claim: Algorithm 1 explicitly uses ASR_paper as a target and triggers a refinement pass when ∆ < τ or ∆ < -10, iterating until the reproduced ASR approaches the reported number. This means the headline '+0.26pp mean deviation' partly reflects a pipeline that is told the answer and optimizes toward it, rather than an independent blind reproduction test of the agents' paper-understanding capability. This conflates 'can the system match a known target number' with 'does the system produce a faithful, paper-correct implementation' — the auditor's line-level fidelity checks mitigate but do not eliminate this concern, since the enhanced refinement pass explicitly does 'gap analysis against sp and R' then patches toward matching ASR.

No human-expert or alternative-tool baseline: there is no controlled comparison against a human engineer's integration time/fidelity, nor against existing frameworks (EasyJailbreak, TeleAI-Safety, OpenRT) performing the same paper-to-module task, so claims that JBF is faster/higher-fidelity than manual integration (the paper's central motivating problem) are not empirically substantiated.

Heavy dependence on official reference repositories undermines the 'freshness' motivation: 22/30 attacks use official code, and the with-repo vs. no-repo ablation shows repos are often essential for fidelity (e.g., GTA δ=+48.6%). Since newly published attacks often lack public code (the exact case JBF claims to solve), the demonstrated fidelity numbers may not generalize well to the paper's stated primary use case.

Reproducibility is compromised by reliance on multiple proprietary, non-open, rapidly-changing agentic tools and models (Cursor Agent, Claude Code, Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex) whose behavior is not independently verifiable or stable over time, making exact replication of the reported pipeline results difficult for other researchers without identical tool access and model versions.

The auditor's acceptance is purely static/line-referenced analysis (never executes code) paired with only a minimal one-sample smoke test as the execution gate (Appendix B.6), which is a fairly weak correctness bar before an implementation is declared '100% fidelity' and entered into the benchmark.

The LOC-reduction and code-reuse metrics (42% reduction, 82.5% reuse) are somewhat unsurprising outcomes of factoring shared scaffolding into a library, and are not benchmarked against what a reasonable human engineer using the same library would achieve, so they don't clearly demonstrate added value from the multi-agent automation itself versus the library design alone.

The attack-model interaction analysis (Section 5) is descriptive and post-hoc, with narrative 'plausible explanation' style interpretations (e.g., deployment-goal trade-off for formal-carrier sensitivity) that are not statistically tested or validated, limiting the rigor of the paper's secondary scientific contribution.

Dual-use and ethical risk (explicitly acknowledged in the Impact Statement) is treated briefly; given that the system automates turning any new jailbreak paper into an executable, benchmark-ready attack module within ~28 minutes, more concrete discussion of release/access controls or mitigations would be warranted given the stated goal of rapid, scalable attack operationalization.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated, practically important problem: jailbreak benchmarks go stale quickly relative to the pace of attack publication, and manual integration is a genuine bottleneck for the field.

Strong empirical validation of reproduction fidelity across 30 diverse attacks spanning multiple search/carrier taxonomy families, with a tight mean ASR deviation of +0.26pp and transparent per-attack breakdown (Table 1), including honest reporting of outlier failures (SCP, ISA).

Useful ablation studies that add credibility and insight: with-repo vs. no-repo reproduction showing where official code matters most (scaffold-heavy methods), and an iteration-count-vs-ASR analysis showing the audit loop doesn't simply inflate results.
The engineering contribution (JBF-LIB) is substantial and measurable: 42% LOC reduction and 82.5% code reuse are concrete, verifiable claims that support the maintainability argument.

The resulting standardized evaluation (30 attacks x 10 victim models) yields genuinely interesting cross-model/cross-attack findings (e.g., mechanism-specific bypasses, carrier-format sensitivity being model-dependent, limited attack transferability) that go beyond simply demonstrating the tool and provide scientific value.

Exceptional transparency in the appendices: full agent prompts, auditor acceptance criteria, and complexity/timing analyses are provided, which substantially aids reproducibility of the pipeline itself.
weaknesses: The auditor performs static analysis only and never executes code; its acceptance criterion (100% fidelity) is binary and based on plan/contract conformance rather than runtime behavioral verification, so subtle behavior-altering bugs could still pass audit despite matching ASR by coincidence.

The 30 reproduced attacks were restricted to papers reporting on AdvBench/JBB with available official repos for most cases (22/30); this is a convenience/feasibility-driven sample that may not generalize to attacks with less clear documentation, non-English prompts, or more complex multi-stage pipelines, limiting claims about general applicability of the +0.26pp fidelity figure.

The 'representative setting' selection methodology (choosing the paper's primary result with the most recent GPT-family model) introduces a researcher-in-the-loop decision that is not automated, slightly undercutting the paper's narrative of an end-to-end automated pipeline producing comparable results without manual effort.

No empirical comparison against general-purpose paper-to-code agents (e.g., Paper2Code, AutoReproduce, PaperBench-style systems) despite being discussed in related work; a head-to-head comparison would better substantiate the claim that domain-specific scaffolding (JBF-LIB) meaningfully outperforms generic approaches on this task.

The pipeline relies on several expensive proprietary frontier models in combination (Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex, plus Claude Code for refinement); no cost/compute analysis is reported, which affects practical reproducibility and the feasibility of the 'living benchmark' vision for other research groups.

The dual-use/ethics discussion is brief and generic ('advocate responsible deployment'); given that the system automates generation of runnable jailbreak code at scale, a more concrete discussion of release/access controls, gating mechanisms, or misuse mitigation would strengthen the ethical treatment.

Some supporting statistical analyses (e.g., iteration-count vs. ASR correlation, with-repo vs. no-repo ablation) are based on small sample sizes (n=2–12 per group, 5 attacks for the ablation), limiting the strength of conclusions drawn from them.

strengths: Addresses a real and timely problem: the manual bottleneck of integrating rapidly evolving jailbreak attacks into standardized benchmarks, motivating a multi-agent (planner-coder-auditor) paper-to-code pipeline specifically tailored to jailbreak attack reproduction.

Extensive empirical validation: 30 reproduced attacks across diverse taxonomy families (search x carrier), with close matched-setting ASR agreement (mean deviation +0.26pp) and thorough supplementary fidelity checks beyond ASR alone (trace-level comparisons, manual semantic fidelity audits with an explicit rubric, LOC decomposition into core vs. scaffolding).

Rich set of ablations and analyses in the appendices: audit-iteration count vs. ASR, planner/coder/auditor backend-model ablation showing the planner role is most sensitive to model quality, token/cost breakdowns, budget-aware ASR-vs-cost plots, and compression ratio interpretation caveats — these substantially strengthen the credibility of the claimed fidelity and efficiency numbers.

The standardized cross-model, cross-attack evaluation (JBF-EVAL heatmap over 30 attacks x 10 victims) yields genuinely interesting and non-trivial findings about model-specific and mechanism-specific vulnerability patterns (e.g., carrier-format sensitivity differences between GPT-5.1 and GPT-OSS-120B), illustrating a concrete downstream benefit of the automated pipeline beyond mere reproduction.

Reasonably transparent about limitations (Future Work), including a specific, appropriate discussion of dual-use/misuse risk and the need to treat papers/repos as untrusted inputs against prompt injection, which is commendable ethical foresight for an automated attack-synthesis system.
weaknesses: The 'representative setting' methodology (choosing one victim model/config per paper matching the paper's primary table) risks selection bias and makes the headline '+0.26pp mean deviation' less informative than it appears; the mean absolute gap of 5.7pp and range of -16% to +20% is arguably the more meaningful number, and it is somewhat buried relative to the headline abstract claim.

Reliance on GPT-4o (and human-in-the-loop 'Human(GPT-4o)') as judge across attacks originally judged very differently (rule-based, human, other LLM judges) introduces judge-substitution confounds that are acknowledged but not deeply quantified — it's unclear how much of the ASR deviation is attributable to judge mismatch vs. genuine implementation fidelity, since these two factors are conflated in the main ∆ metric.

The 'high fidelity' claims rest partly on an auditor that is itself an LLM performing purely static, non-executing analysis (Appendix B.6), which is a comparatively weak form of verification; the acceptance criterion (100% fidelity threshold) is somewhat self-referential/circular for validating the system's own core claims, and the manual semantic audit in Appendix F, while a nice addition, only covers 4 of 30 attacks.

Cost and scalability of the pipeline (millions of tokens, multiple expensive frontier-model backends: Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex, plus Claude Code for refinement) are non-trivial and could limit practical 'living benchmark' adoption by less resourced labs; the framing of the system as broadly scalable is somewhat understated relative to this cost.

Significant engineering contribution but modest methodological/scientific novelty: the system largely combines existing ideas (agentic paper-to-code translation, LLM-as-judge, standardized harnesses) into a jailbreak-specific instantiation; the core research insight is more infrastructural than conceptual, and closely related concurrent frameworks (EasyJailbreak, TeleAI-Safety, OpenRT) are only briefly differentiated.

Coverage is restricted to AdvBench/JailbreakBench, black-box/gray-box text-only single/multi-turn attacks (excluding white-box and multimodal), which is reasonable scope-wise but means claims of enabling 'living benchmarks' for the full jailbreak literature are somewhat overstated relative to what is actually demonstrated.

strengths: The empirical scope is substantial: 30 reproduced attacks spanning five carrier types and four search strategies, evaluated against 10 victim models, with extensive appendices covering ablations (agent backend sensitivity, iteration-count correlation, LOC/token cost breakdowns, budget-aware ASR analysis).

The taxonomy of jailbreak attacks (search x carrier axes) is a useful organizing contribution independent of the system itself, and is used consistently to structure the cross-model analysis in Section 5.

The paper goes beyond headline ASR-deviation numbers with some complementary fidelity checks: trace-level comparisons (Past-Tense, QueryAttack) and a manual semantic fidelity audit with an explicit rubric (Appendix F), which partially addresses the concern that ASR alone is a weak proxy for implementation correctness.

The cross-model heatmap (Figure 4) surfaces genuinely interesting phenomena (e.g., GPT-OSS-120B's narrow blind spots, carrier-format sensitivity differences across models) that illustrate the practical value of having many attacks evaluated under one harness.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a fairly standard planner-coder-auditor LLM-agent pipeline (a pattern already explored in Paper2Code, PaperBench, AutoReproduce, and other paper-to-code work cited in Section 2) applied to a narrower domain (jailbreak attacks). The paper does not clearly articulate what is methodologically novel about JBF-FORGE beyond domain-specific prompt engineering and a shared contract library; this reads more as an applied engineering/benchmarking exercise than a research contribution appropriate for the main ICML track.

Fidelity verification is largely circular: the auditor that determines '100% fidelity' acceptance is itself an LLM (GPT-5.1 Codex), auditing code written by another LLM (Claude-4.5-Sonnet) against a plan written by a third LLM (Gemini-3-pro). Beyond the 4-attack manual semantic audit in Appendix F, there is no independent human ground-truth verification of the bulk of the 30 reproduced attacks, undermining confidence in the headline '+0.26 pp mean deviation' and '100% fidelity acceptance' claims.

The pipeline depends entirely on closed, proprietary, frequently-updated commercial models and agent products (Cursor Agent, Claude Code, Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex, Kimi-K2.5). This makes the system difficult to reproduce by third parties (behavior will drift as these APIs are updated/deprecated), and undercuts the paper's own stated goal of enabling reproducible, longitudinal benchmarking — the pipeline itself is not a stable, versioned artifact.

ASR fidelity is reported with a favorable framing (mean signed deviation +0.26 pp) that masks substantial per-attack variance (mean absolute deviation 5.7 pp, with several attacks off by -16 to +20 pp). The 'representative setting' selection procedure (choosing the paper's primary table result with the most recent GPT-family model) introduces discretionary judgment that is not independently validated and could bias comparability.

No real baseline comparison is provided against manual integration effort (e.g., actual engineer-hours for existing frameworks like EasyJailbreak/OpenRT) or against simpler single-agent paper-to-code baselines; the claimed '58% LOC reduction' and '28.2 minute' integration time are compared only to the original authors' repositories, which is not an apples-to-apples baseline for the paper's central claim of outperforming manual integration pipelines.

Judging methodology mixes protocols inconsistently: paper-matched ASR reproduction uses each paper's original judge (GPT-4, human-as-GPT-4o proxies, LLaMA-based judges, etc.), while the standardized JBF-EVAL benchmark uses a single GPT-4o judge; known unreliability and prompt-sensitivity of LLM-as-judge is not analyzed or calibrated against human labels anywhere in the main paper.

The study is restricted to AdvBench/JBB and black-box/gray-box, single-turn-dominant, text-only attacks; this is a reasonable scoping decision but substantially narrows claimed generality ('living benchmarks that keep pace with the shifting security landscape') relative to the broad framing in the abstract and introduction.

Presentation is heavily backloaded: the 9-page main body is thin on methodological detail (e.g., Algorithm 1 is underspecified about how REFINE and the enhanced pass concretely change behavior), while ~34 pages of appendices (including full verbatim agent prompts) carry most of the substantive evidence, making the core contribution hard to assess from the main text alone.

Dual-use/ethical risk is acknowledged only briefly in the Impact Statement and deferred to 'future work' (sandboxing, adversarial-input hardening); given that the system's explicit purpose is to automatically translate jailbreak papers into runnable, scaled attack code, the lack of any current safeguard or responsible-disclosure protocol is a notable gap for a paper whose main artifact is attack automation.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely problem: jailbreak benchmarks go stale quickly relative to the pace of new attack papers, and existing frameworks rely on slow manual integration.

The system (JBF-LIB, JBF-FORGE, JBF-EVAL) is well-engineered and clearly described, with a concrete planner-coder-auditor loop, explicit contract/registry design, and full prompts provided in the appendix for reproducibility of the pipeline itself.

Extensive empirical validation beyond headline ASR numbers: mean ASR deviation of +0.26pp across 30 attacks, trace-/mechanism-level checks (Appendix F), a manual semantic fidelity audit with an explicit rubric, and a with-repo vs. no-repo ablation isolating the value of reference code.

Thoughtful self-critical appendices that preempt obvious objections, e.g., Appendix G decomposes the LOC compression ratio into core-attack-logic vs. scaffolding to show fidelity isn't conflated with code shrinkage, and Appendix H adds a budget/token-aware view of ASR.

The standardized cross-model, cross-attack AdvBench evaluation (30 attacks x 10 victims under one judge) is itself a useful contribution, surfacing non-trivial findings about model-specific blind spots, carrier-format sensitivity, and limited attack transferability that would be invisible under siloed single-paper evaluations.

Planner/coder/auditor model ablation (Appendix E) and iteration-count-vs-ASR analysis (Appendix C) add useful mechanistic understanding of what drives the pipeline's success, rather than treating it as a black box.
weaknesses: The auditor's 'fidelity' verification is itself an LLM performing static code review against an LLM-generated plan; this is somewhat circular (the same pipeline grades its own output) and the paper does not evaluate auditor reliability independently (e.g., auditor agreement with human experts, false-accept rates) beyond the post-hoc manual semantic audit on only 4 attacks.

The attack set is restricted to papers reporting AdvBench/JBB results, which may bias the sample toward attacks that are easier to standardize and could overstate general applicability of the fidelity numbers; white-box, multimodal, and attacks without clean single-dataset reporting are excluded by design.

Main fidelity/ASR results are single-run, paper-matched point estimates without variance/confidence intervals despite acknowledged stochasticity in jailbreak evaluation and API nondeterminism, making it hard to judge whether small deltas (e.g., +0.26pp mean) are meaningful versus noise.

Standardizing all cross-model results on a single GPT-4o judge is a strong simplification; judge-model drift, judge gameability, and sensitivity of comparative conclusions (Section 5) to the choice of judge are not stress-tested.

The pipeline's cost and reproducibility depend heavily on specific proprietary backend models (Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex, Claude Code) that are expensive, change over time, and are not independently verifiable by other labs, which is somewhat in tension with the paper's reproducibility framing.

Token/cost analysis (Appendix D) shows several million tokens per attack, which, combined with closed-model dependence, raises practical questions about the scalability and accessibility claims ("28.2 minutes... without manual implementation effort") that are not fully reconciled with actual monetary/API cost.

The dual-use/ethical risk (automating creation of runnable jailbreak attacks at scale) is acknowledged but mitigations (sandboxing, prompt-injection resistance) are deferred entirely to future work, leaving the current released system's safeguards unspecified.
